title: NATO's First Ultimatum: The August 1993 Air Strike Threat
content:
Throughout the summer of 1993, the siege of Sarajevo reached a new level of intensity as VRS forces tightened their grip on the heights surrounding the city. Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica, the last overland routes connecting Sarajevo to government-held central Bosnia, came under sustained VRS assault in late July, threatening to seal the capital's encirclement entirely. The offensive prompted an international reaction that marked a turning point in the Alliance's posture toward the Bosnian War.

On 9 August 1993, NATO's North Atlantic Council authorized the preparation of air strikes against Bosnian Serb positions threatening Sarajevo and the UN-designated safe areas. This was a historic threshold: the first time in its forty-four-year existence that NATO had approved the potential use of offensive military force. The decision came after months of escalating rhetoric from Western governments, driven by sustained media coverage of the Sarajevo siege and growing political pressure from publics horrified by the continuing bombardment of a European capital.

The operational framework, however, severely constrained the threat's credibility. Under the so-called "dual-key" arrangement, any air strike required authorization from both NATO's military command and the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative in the former Yugoslavia. The UN chain of command prioritized the safety of UNPROFOR personnel and the continuation of humanitarian operations, making execution politically uncertain even after authorization.

The Council decision recorded a coercive threat, not the disposition of Mount Igman. The RS leadership's separate Lukavac decision determines whether the captured positions are vacated or held. If the operation predicate is absent, the authorization still belongs in the historical record without implying that any campaign withdrawal occurred.
